uhiExplainer.title1: What is the urban heat island
uhiExplainer.p1: Cities are hotter than the surrounding countryside. Asphalt, concrete, and dark roofs absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly at night; the lack of vegetation reduces the evapotranspiration that normally cools the air; building density traps heat and reduces ventilation. The result is a thermal differential — the urban heat island (UHI) — that can exceed 4–5°C compared to nearby rural areas, especially on summer nights.
uhiExplainer.li1: Dark impermeable surfaces absorb more solar energy (low albedo).
uhiExplainer.li3: Urban geometry (street canyons between buildings) traps heat and reduces nighttime dispersion.
uhiExplainer.li4: Anthropogenic heat: traffic, industry, air conditioners.
uhiExplainer.p2: Tropical nights (minimum above 20°C) prevent physiological recovery from daytime heat and increase the risk of heat stress, especially for the elderly, children, and people with cardiovascular or respiratory conditions. UHI amplifies this risk exactly where population density is highest.
uhiExplainer.title4: Why it pays to act now, not wait
uhiExplainer.p3: Heatwaves in Europe have become more frequent and intense in recent decades (IPCC, Sixth Assessment Report, 2021): it's not a problem that resolves itself, it accumulates summer after summer. Every year without action is one more year in which the air-conditioning vicious cycle (see a city's detail panel) keeps getting worse — and one more year of full bills before any investment starts paying for itself (see "payback" in the cost estimator). Many home interventions (reflective paint, climbing plants, a tree) cost little and don't need an urban plan to get started — you can start with a single roof. Postponing isn't a neutral choice — it's the choice to keep paying for the problem instead of reducing it.

albedoExplainer.p1: Albedo is the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects instead of absorbing. It ranges from 0 (absorbs everything, perfect black) to 1 (reflects everything, perfect white).
albedoExplainer.p2: A dark roof (albedo ~0.1) reaches 70–80°C surface temperature at noon. At night it releases that accumulated heat for hours — like having a radiator running on the ceiling. A white roof (albedo ~0.75) reaches 35–45°C: it has 50–60% less thermal energy to release, and the city cools down faster after sunset.

infoPanel.title: Urban heat islands in Italy
infoPanel.methodologyText: The UHI values shown on the map are model estimates, not direct measurements, calculated from population, latitude, coastal proximity, and Po Valley position. The satellite layers (Copernicus Sentinel Hub) show real surface temperature, with ~2 days of latency. Costs and savings are order-of-magnitude figures at city scale, not quotes.

fire.title: What to do in case of wildfire
fire.p1: If you spot flames or even just smoke, call 115 (Fire Department) or 112 (single emergency number) immediately. State precisely where you are — municipality, locality, landmarks — and don't hang up until the operator tells you to. Don't assume someone else has already reported it.
fire.p2: If you're caught in the fire: look for an escape route toward a road or waterway, never move downwind (in the direction the fire is being pushed by wind) — you risk being trapped. If surrounded, lie down in an area without vegetation: smoke tends to rise. If possible, cross the fire front at its weakest point to reach the already-burned area, which is safer. Don't stop along roads to watch: it hinders rescue operations.
fire.p3: Prevention: never throw away lit cigarette butts or matches — they're enough to ignite dry grass. Don't light fires outside designated areas, and never when it's windy. If you park your car on dry grass, check that the exhaust doesn't touch it. Don't burn agricultural residue without proper precautions.
fire.redCross: The Italian Red Cross is part of the national Civil Protection system and provides social-health assistance, reception, and support in wildfire fighting (AIB) too — but it's not the number to call first: the initial report always goes to 115/112.
fire.source: Source: <a1>Department of Civil Protection</a1> and <a2>Io Non Rischio</a2>.

earthquake.title: What to do in case of an earthquake
earthquake.p1: During the shaking, indoors: shelter in a doorway on a load-bearing wall, under a sturdy table or bed, or next to a load-bearing wall. Don't use stairs or the elevator.
earthquake.p2: During the shaking, outdoors: move away from buildings, trees, lampposts, and power lines. In a car, don't stop near bridges, landslide-prone ground, or beaches.
earthquake.p3: After the shaking: check on people near you, without moving anyone severely injured. Turn off gas, water, and power. Go outside carefully wearing shoes, reach an open space away from buildings, avoid elevators and damaged stairs. If you're near the coast and the shaking was strong: move away from the beach and reach higher ground (tsunami risk).
earthquake.p4: Number to call: 112 (single emergency number), which routes to 115 (Fire Department, technical rescue/extraction) or 118 (medical emergency) depending on need.
earthquake.redCross: The Italian Red Cross is part of the national Civil Protection system and provides social-health assistance, reception centers, and field hospitals after the event — but it's not the number to call first: the initial report always goes to 112.
earthquake.source: Source: <a1>Department of Civil Protection</a1> and <a2>Io Non Rischio</a2>.

hydroRisk.floodTitle: What to do in case of a flood
hydroRisk.p1: Indoors: don't go down to basements, cellars, or garages to save belongings — they're the most dangerous areas. Go to upper floors, avoid the elevator, turn off gas and electrical systems. Don't drink tap water: it could be contaminated.
hydroRisk.p2: Outdoors: move away from the flooded area — water flows faster than it looks. Avoid using a car: just a few centimeters of water can make you lose control. Avoid underpasses and embankments.
hydroRisk.p3: Afterward: wait for authorities' clearance before returning, don't drive on flooded roads (possible potholes or open manholes), check gas and electricity before turning them back on, don't eat food that came into contact with floodwater.
hydroRisk.landslideTitle: What to do in case of a landslide
hydroRisk.p4: Warning signs: small cracks or fractures in walls, walls rotating or shifting. If the landslide is moving toward you, move immediately to higher, stable ground — if you can't escape, curl up and protect your head. Watch for bouncing rocks or debris, don't stay under poles or pylons, stay away from streams and torrents (mudflow risk). After the event, report any trapped people to rescuers without entering the landslide area yourself.
hydroRisk.redCross: The Italian Red Cross is part of the national Civil Protection system and provides social-health assistance and reception after the event — but it's not the number to call first.
hydroRisk.source: Source: <a1>Department of Civil Protection — floods</a1> and <a2>landslides</a2>.
